summary.en: English fixes the order of subject, verb and object, and that fixed order is what carries the meaning Russian carries with endings. How questions and negatives are built from an auxiliary rather than by moving words around.
summary.ru: В английском порядок подлежащего, глагола и дополнения закреплён, и именно он несёт смысл, который в русском несут окончания. Как из вспомогательного глагола строятся вопросы и отрицания.

body.en:
English words do not change shape to show who did what. `The dog bit the man` and `The man bit the dog` are built from the same five words; only the order tells you who ended up at the hospital. Russian marks the roles with endings and can move the words freely — English cannot, and that single fact drives most of what follows.

## Subject, verb, object, in that order

The core of an English statement is **subject - verb - object**, and nothing may be dropped:

```
Anna reads books.
My brother bought a car.
```

Two consequences catch Russian speakers out.

First, the subject is never left out. Russian says `Холодно` with no subject; English needs a placeholder — `It is cold`, not `Is cold`. The `it` means nothing at all, it just fills the slot.

Second, the verb is never left out either. Russian drops the present tense of "to be"; English keeps it. `Она врач` is `She **is** a doctor`.

## Where everything else goes

Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb but after `be`:

```
I often work late.
She is often late.
```

Manner, place and time cluster after the object, and in that order:

```
We played football badly in the park yesterday.
```

Nothing may sit between the verb and its object. `I like very much this film` is wrong; `I like this film very much` is right.

## Questions need an auxiliary

Russian turns a statement into a question with intonation alone. English inverts the subject and an **auxiliary** verb. If the statement has no auxiliary, `do` is inserted to be inverted:

```
You work here.      ->  Do you work here?
She works here.     ->  Does she work here?
You worked here.    ->  Did you work here?
```

Once `do` carries the tense, the main verb goes back to its plain form: `Does she **work**`, never `Does she works`. The tense is marked once, on the auxiliary.

`be` needs no helper, because it can invert on its own: `She is late` -> `Is she late?`

Question words go in front of that whole structure: `Where do you work?` The one exception is when the question word *is* the subject — then there is nothing to invert, and the order stays as in a statement:

```
Who lives here?          (not: Who does live here?)
What happened?
```

## Negatives work the same way

Negation attaches to the auxiliary, not to the main verb:

```
I do not know.     I don't know.
She does not know. She doesn't know.
He is not here.    He isn't here.
```

And English negates once. Russian stacks negatives — `Я никогда никому ничего не говорил` — where English allows exactly one: `I never told anyone anything`. Two negatives cancel out instead of reinforcing.
body.ru:
Английские слова не меняют форму, чтобы показать, кто что сделал. `The dog bit the man` и `The man bit the dog` собраны из одних и тех же пяти слов; кто попал в больницу, говорит только порядок. Русский помечает роли окончаниями и может двигать слова свободно — английский не может, и из этого одного факта вытекает почти всё дальнейшее.

## Подлежащее, глагол, дополнение — в этом порядке

Ядро английского утверждения — **подлежащее - глагол - дополнение**, и выбросить нельзя ничего:

```
Anna reads books.
My brother bought a car.
```

Отсюда два следствия, на которых спотыкаются русскоговорящие.

Во-первых, подлежащее не опускается. По-русски можно сказать `Холодно` без подлежащего; английскому нужна заглушка — `It is cold`, а не `Is cold`. Это `it` не значит вообще ничего, оно просто занимает место.

Во-вторых, глагол тоже не опускается. Русский выбрасывает «быть» в настоящем времени; английский его держит. `Она врач` — это `She **is** a doctor`.

## Куда встаёт всё остальное

Наречия частоты — перед смысловым глаголом, но после `be`:

```
I often work late.
She is often late.
```

Образ действия, место и время идут после дополнения, и именно в таком порядке:

```
We played football badly in the park yesterday.
```

Между глаголом и его дополнением не встаёт ничего. `I like very much this film` — неверно; `I like this film very much` — верно.

## Вопросу нужен вспомогательный глагол

Русский превращает утверждение в вопрос одной интонацией. Английский меняет местами подлежащее и **вспомогательный** глагол. Если в утверждении вспомогательного нет, вставляется `do` — чтобы было что переставлять:

```
You work here.      ->  Do you work here?
She works here.     ->  Does she work here?
You worked here.    ->  Did you work here?
```

Как только `do` берёт на себя время, смысловой глагол возвращается в исходную форму: `Does she **work**`, но не `Does she works`. Время помечается один раз — на вспомогательном.

`be` помощник не нужен, он переставляется сам: `She is late` -> `Is she late?`

Вопросительное слово встаёт перед всей этой конструкцией: `Where do you work?` Исключение одно — когда вопросительное слово *и есть* подлежащее. Тогда переставлять нечего, и порядок остаётся как в утверждении:

```
Who lives here?          (не: Who does live here?)
What happened?
```

## Отрицание работает так же

Отрицание цепляется к вспомогательному глаголу, а не к смысловому:

```
I do not know.     I don't know.
She does not know. She doesn't know.
He is not here.    He isn't here.
```

И отрицает английский один раз. Русский копит отрицания — `Я никогда никому ничего не говорил`, — а английский допускает ровно одно: `I never told anyone anything`. Два отрицания не усиливают друг друга, а взаимно уничтожаются.

summary.en: The verb English never drops, the two ways of saying you own something, and the there is/there are pattern that announces existence rather than location.
summary.ru: Глагол, который английский никогда не выбрасывает, два способа сказать «у меня есть» и конструкция there is/there are, которая сообщает о существовании, а не о месте.

body.en:
`be` is the verb Russian leaves out and English cannot. It is also the most irregular verb in the language, which is why it is worth learning as a table rather than as a rule.

## be

```
I am            I'm            am I?        I'm not
you/we/they are you're/we're   are you?     you aren't
he/she/it is    he's/she's     is he?       he isn't
```

The past has just two forms: `was` for I/he/she/it, `were` for you/we/they.

`be` needs no auxiliary. It makes its own questions by inverting and its own negatives by taking `not`, which is why `Is she a doctor?` needs no `do` anywhere.

Watch the places English uses `be` where Russian uses a different verb entirely. Age is `be`, not `have`: `I **am** 30`, never `I have 30 years`. So are hunger, cold and fear when they describe a person: `I'm hungry`, `I'm cold`, `I'm afraid`.

## have got and have

Both say you own or possess something. `have got` is more spoken and more British; plain `have` is neutral and works everywhere:

```
I've got a car.        =  I have a car.
Have you got a car?    =  Do you have a car?
I haven't got a car.   =  I don't have a car.
```

Note which word carries the question. With `have got` the auxiliary is `have`, so it inverts by itself. With plain `have` there is no auxiliary, so `do` is needed — the ordinary rule.

`have got` exists only in the present. The past is `had` for both: `I had a car`, `Did you have a car?` There is no `had got` meaning possession.

And `have got` is only for possession and relationships. When `have` means an action — having breakfast, having a shower, having a good time — `got` is impossible: `I have breakfast at eight`, never `I've got breakfast at eight`.

## there is and there are

To say that something **exists** somewhere, English announces it with `there`:

```
There is a book on the table.
There are two books on the table.
```

The verb agrees with what follows it, not with `there`: `there **is** a book`, `there **are** books`. In a list, it agrees with the first item: `There is a book and two pens on the table`.

This `there` is not the `there` that means "in that place". Both can appear in one sentence without redundancy: `There is a shop over there`.

The difference from `it is` is worth pinning down, because Russian uses one pattern for both. `There is` introduces something new; `it is` says something about a thing already known:

```
There is a car outside.     (announcing it - you did not know)
It is my brother's car.     (describing the car we just mentioned)
```

Starting with `It is a car outside` is the mistake this contrast prevents.
body.ru:
`be` — тот самый глагол, который русский выбрасывает, а английский не может. Он же самый нерегулярный в языке, поэтому его выгоднее выучить таблицей, а не правилом.

## be

```
I am            I'm            am I?        I'm not
you/we/they are you're/we're   are you?     you aren't
he/she/it is    he's/she's     is he?       he isn't
```

В прошедшем всего две формы: `was` для I/he/she/it и `were` для you/we/they.

`be` не нужен вспомогательный глагол. Вопрос он делает сам перестановкой, отрицание — через `not`, поэтому в `Is she a doctor?` никакого `do` нет и не должно быть.

Отдельно стоит следить за местами, где английский берёт `be`, а русский — совсем другой глагол. Возраст — это `be`, а не `have`: `I **am** 30`, но никогда `I have 30 years`. Так же устроены голод, холод и страх, когда речь о человеке: `I'm hungry`, `I'm cold`, `I'm afraid`.

## have got и have

Оба означают «иметь». `have got` разговорнее и более британское; простое `have` нейтрально и годится везде:

```
I've got a car.        =  I have a car.
Have you got a car?    =  Do you have a car?
I haven't got a car.   =  I don't have a car.
```

Обратите внимание, какое слово несёт вопрос. У `have got` вспомогательный — `have`, он переставляется сам. У простого `have` вспомогательного нет, поэтому нужен `do` — обычное правило.

`have got` существует только в настоящем. Прошедшее у обоих — `had`: `I had a car`, `Did you have a car?` Никакого `had got` в значении «имел» нет.

И `have got` — только про обладание и родство. Когда `have` означает действие — завтракать, принимать душ, хорошо проводить время, — `got` невозможен: `I have breakfast at eight`, но не `I've got breakfast at eight`.

## there is и there are

Чтобы сказать, что что-то **существует** где-то, английский объявляет это через `there`:

```
There is a book on the table.
There are two books on the table.
```

Глагол согласуется с тем, что стоит после него, а не с `there`: `there **is** a book`, `there **are** books`. В перечислении — с первым элементом: `There is a book and two pens on the table`.

Это `there` — не то `there`, которое значит «там». Оба могут стоять в одном предложении без всякой тавтологии: `There is a shop over there`.

Разницу с `it is` стоит закрепить, потому что русский обходится одной конструкцией на оба случая. `There is` вводит что-то новое; `it is` говорит что-то о уже известном:

```
There is a car outside.     (сообщаем - вы не знали)
It is my brother's car.     (описываем машину, о которой только что сказали)
```

Начать с `It is a car outside` — как раз та ошибка, от которой спасает это противопоставление.

summary.en: How plurals are formed and where the irregulars are, and the countable/uncountable split that decides which article, which quantifier and which verb form a noun can take.
summary.ru: Как образуется множественное число и где нерегулярные формы, и деление на исчисляемые и неисчисляемые, от которого зависят артикль, квантификатор и форма глагола.

body.en:
Most English plurals are an `-s` away. The reason nouns get a section of their own is the second question they raise: whether the thing can be counted at all. That answer decides the article, the quantifier and the verb.

## Forming the plural

Add `-s`. Then the spelling adjustments:

```
-s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -o  ->  -es      bus/buses, box/boxes, potato/potatoes
consonant + -y             ->  -ies     city/cities  (but: boy/boys)
-f, -fe                    ->  -ves     knife/knives, leaf/leaves
```

The irregulars are a short list worth memorising outright, because they are all common words:

```
man/men      woman/women    child/children   person/people
foot/feet    tooth/teeth    mouse/mice       goose/geese
sheep/sheep  fish/fish      series/series
```

## Countable and uncountable

A **countable** noun can be counted: one book, two books. An **uncountable** noun cannot: water, music, advice. Uncountable nouns have no plural and take a singular verb.

That means an uncountable noun cannot take `a/an` and cannot take a number. To count it, you count a container or a portion instead:

```
a piece of advice        two pieces of advice
a glass of water         three glasses of water
a bit of luck
```

## The ones that surprise Russian speakers

The split is not about physical substance — it is a grammatical fact about each word, and the two languages disagree on several very common ones. These are uncountable in English but countable in Russian:

```
advice     information   news       knowledge
money      furniture     luggage    equipment
work       research      progress   traffic
bread      hair          weather
```

So: `Her advice **was** useful`, not `were`. `The news **is** bad`, despite the `-s`. `I need some information`, never `an information` or `informations`.

The other direction is rarer but real: `hair` is uncountable as the stuff on your head (`My hair **is** long`) and countable as individual strands (`There are two hairs in my soup`).

## Always plural

Some nouns exist only in the plural, and most of them are things made of two matching halves:

```
trousers   jeans   glasses   scissors   clothes   people
```

They take a plural verb — `My trousers **are** dirty` — and to count them you need `a pair of`: `two pairs of jeans`.

`people` deserves its own line: it is the ordinary plural of `person`, takes a plural verb (`People **are** waiting`), and `peoples` exists only in the separate sense of nations.
body.ru:
Большинство английских множественных чисел — это плюс `-s`. Отдельный раздел существительным нужен из-за второго вопроса, который они поднимают: можно ли это вообще посчитать. От ответа зависят артикль, квантификатор и глагол.

## Образование множественного числа

Добавляем `-s`. Дальше — правки орфографии:

```
-s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -o  ->  -es      bus/buses, box/boxes, potato/potatoes
согласная + -y             ->  -ies     city/cities  (но: boy/boys)
-f, -fe                    ->  -ves     knife/knives, leaf/leaves
```

Нерегулярные — короткий список, который стоит просто выучить, потому что все слова частотные:

```
man/men      woman/women    child/children   person/people
foot/feet    tooth/teeth    mouse/mice       goose/geese
sheep/sheep  fish/fish      series/series
```

## Исчисляемые и неисчисляемые

**Исчисляемое** существительное можно посчитать: одна книга, две книги. **Неисчисляемое** — нельзя: вода, музыка, совет. У неисчисляемых нет множественного числа, и глагол при них в единственном.

Значит, неисчисляемое не берёт `a/an` и не берёт числительное. Чтобы его посчитать, считают ёмкость или порцию:

```
a piece of advice        two pieces of advice
a glass of water         three glasses of water
a bit of luck
```

## Те, что удивляют русскоговорящих

Деление не про физическую природу вещества — это грамматический факт о каждом конкретном слове, и по нескольким очень частотным словам два языка расходятся. Вот неисчисляемые в английском, но исчисляемые в русском:

```
advice     information   news       knowledge
money      furniture     luggage    equipment
work       research      progress   traffic
bread      hair          weather
```

Отсюда: `Her advice **was** useful`, а не `were`. `The news **is** bad` — несмотря на `-s`. `I need some information`, но никогда `an information` или `informations`.

Обратное направление встречается реже, но существует: `hair` неисчисляемо как то, что растёт на голове (`My hair **is** long`), и исчисляемо как отдельные волоски (`There are two hairs in my soup`).

## Всегда множественные

Некоторые существительные существуют только во множественном, и большинство из них — предметы из двух одинаковых половин:

```
trousers   jeans   glasses   scissors   clothes   people
```

Глагол при них множественный — `My trousers **are** dirty`, — а чтобы посчитать, нужен `a pair of`: `two pairs of jeans`.

`people` заслуживает отдельной строки: это обычное множественное от `person`, глагол при нём множественный (`People **are** waiting`), а `peoples` существует только в отдельном значении «народы».

summary.en: The article system Russian has no equivalent for: a/an for one of many, the for the one we both mean, and no article at all for things in general.
summary.ru: Система артиклей, которой в русском нет вовсе: a/an для «одного из многих», the для «того самого» и отсутствие артикля для вещей вообще.

body.en:
Russian has no articles, so this is not a rule to adjust but a distinction to build from scratch. The good news is that it reduces to one question asked before every noun: **does my listener already know which one I mean?**

## a/an - one of many

`a` introduces something the listener does not yet know about, or says what kind of thing something is:

```
I bought a book.          (you don't know which one yet)
She is a doctor.          (what kind of person she is)
```

`an` before a vowel *sound*, not a vowel letter. The sound is what counts: `an hour` (the h is silent), `a university` (it starts with a "yu" sound), `an MP` (the letter M is read "em").

`a/an` means "one", so it is impossible with plurals and with uncountables. There is no `a books` and no `an advice`.

## the - the one we both mean

`the` says the listener can identify which one. There are four common ways they can:

```
It was mentioned before:   I bought a book. The book was expensive.
The situation makes it obvious: Close the door. (the one in this room)
It is described:           the book I told you about
There is only one:         the sun, the moon, the President
```

`the` is also how you point at a superlative or an ordinal, because both single out exactly one: `the best film`, `the first time`.

## No article at all

Bare plural and bare uncountable nouns mean the category in general. This is the one Russian speakers under-use, because Russian has nothing to omit:

```
Books are expensive.        (books in general)
I like music.               (music in general)
Water boils at 100C.
```

Compare the three:

```
I need a chair.        one, any one
I need the chair.      that specific one
I like chairs.         chairs as a category
```

No article also goes with meals, most countries and cities, languages, months and days, and with `go to bed / school / work / hospital` when they mean the activity rather than the building:

```
I have breakfast at eight.      He speaks Russian.
She's in hospital.              (she is ill)
She's at the hospital.          (she is there, perhaps visiting)
```

## Where mistakes cluster

Two patterns cause most of the errors:

**A singular countable noun needs an article.** It cannot stand bare. `I am student` is wrong; `I am **a** student`. If a singular countable noun has no `a/an`, it needs `the`, `my`, `this` or a number — something.

**Professions take `a`.** `She is a teacher`, `He wants to be a lawyer`. Russian omits the article here and the habit carries over hard.

Learn the fixed phrases as phrases rather than deriving them: `at home`, `by car`, `on foot`, `in the morning`, `at night`, `last year`, `next week`.
body.ru:
В русском артиклей нет, так что это не правило, которое нужно подправить, а различение, которое нужно построить с нуля. Хорошая новость: всё сводится к одному вопросу перед каждым существительным — **знает ли мой слушатель, о каком именно предмете речь?**

## a/an — один из многих

`a` вводит то, о чём слушатель ещё не знает, или сообщает, что это за вещь:

```
I bought a book.          (вы пока не знаете, какую)
She is a doctor.          (кто она по профессии)
```

`an` — перед гласным *звуком*, а не гласной буквой. Считается именно звук: `an hour` (h не читается), `a university` (начинается со звука «ю»), `an MP` (буква M читается «эм»).

`a/an` значит «один», поэтому с множественным числом и с неисчисляемыми он невозможен. Нет ни `a books`, ни `an advice`.

## the — тот самый

`the` сообщает, что слушатель может опознать, о каком предмете речь. Опознать он может четырьмя обычными способами:

```
О нём уже говорили:      I bought a book. The book was expensive.
Ситуация делает очевидным: Close the door. (ту, что в этой комнате)
Его описывают:            the book I told you about
Он такой один:            the sun, the moon, the President
```

Через `the` же указывают на превосходную степень и на порядковое числительное — оба выделяют ровно один предмет: `the best film`, `the first time`.

## Вообще без артикля

Существительное во множественном или неисчисляемое без артикля означает категорию вообще. Именно этот случай русскоговорящие недоиспользуют — в русском нечего опускать:

```
Books are expensive.        (книги вообще)
I like music.               (музыка вообще)
Water boils at 100C.
```

Сравните три:

```
I need a chair.        какой-нибудь, любой
I need the chair.      тот самый
I like chairs.         стулья как категория
```

Без артикля идут также приёмы пищи, большинство стран и городов, языки, месяцы и дни недели, а ещё `go to bed / school / work / hospital`, когда речь о занятии, а не о здании:

```
I have breakfast at eight.      He speaks Russian.
She's in hospital.              (она болеет)
She's at the hospital.          (она там, например пришла навестить)
```

## Где скапливаются ошибки

Основную часть ошибок дают два случая.

**Исчисляемому в единственном числе артикль нужен.** Само оно стоять не может. `I am student` — неверно; `I am **a** student`. Если у исчисляемого в единственном нет `a/an`, значит нужен `the`, `my`, `this` или числительное — хоть что-то.

**Профессии берут `a`.** `She is a teacher`, `He wants to be a lawyer`. Русский здесь артикль опускает, и привычка переносится очень упорно.

Устойчивые выражения выгоднее учить как выражения, а не выводить: `at home`, `by car`, `on foot`, `in the morning`, `at night`, `last year`, `next week`.

summary.en: Subject and object pronouns, the two ways to show possession and why English needs one where Russian does not, and this/that/these/those.
summary.ru: Местоимения в роли подлежащего и дополнения, два способа выразить принадлежность и почему английскому он нужен там, где русскому нет, и this/that/these/those.

body.en:
Pronouns are where English keeps the case endings it lost everywhere else. `I` and `me` are the same word in two roles, and the role is fixed by position.

## Subject and object

```
subject   I     you    he    she   it    we    they
object    me    you    him   her   it    us    them
```

The subject form goes before the verb, the object form after a verb or a preposition:

```
I saw her.          She saw me.
Give it to him.     Come with us.
```

After a preposition it is always the object form — `between you and **me**`, never `between you and I`.

## Possessive: two forms, two jobs

```
before a noun    my    your   his   her   its    our   their
standing alone   mine  yours  his   hers  -      ours  theirs
```

```
This is my car.        This car is mine.
Her book is here.      This book is hers.
```

The second column is what you use when the noun is understood, which is why `mine` never has a noun after it. `This is mine car` is the error to watch.

Two spelling traps that matter more than they look:

- **`its` vs `it's`.** `its` is possessive (`the dog and its bone`); `it's` is `it is`. There is no apostrophe in the possessive.
- **`your` vs `you're`.** Same split, same reason.

## The apostrophe on nouns

For people and animals, possession goes on the noun:

```
Anna's book         the boy's dog
the boys' dogs      (plural already ends in -s, so just the apostrophe)
the children's toys (irregular plural, so 's)
```

For things, English prefers `of`: `the leg of the table`, not `the table's leg`.

## Reflexive

```
myself  yourself  himself  herself  itself  ourselves  yourselves  themselves
```

Used when subject and object are the same person: `I hurt myself`, `She taught herself Spanish`. Also for emphasis: `I did it myself`.

The trap is that some English verbs are not reflexive where the Russian ones are. `Wash`, `dress`, `shave`, `feel`, `relax`, `concentrate`, `meet` take no reflexive: `I feel bad`, never `I feel myself bad` — which means something quite different and best avoided.

## this, that, these, those

```
near    this (one)    these (many)
far     that (one)    those (many)
```

Near and far can be about place, but also about time and attitude: `this week` is the one we are in, `that year` is a year that is over.

They work as determiners (`this book`) and as pronouns on their own (`This is my book`). And they carry number, so they must agree: `these books`, never `this books`.
body.ru:
Местоимения — то место, где английский сохранил падежи, потерянные во всём остальном. `I` и `me` — одно слово в двух ролях, а роль задаётся позицией.

## Подлежащее и дополнение

```
подлежащее   I     you    he    she   it    we    they
дополнение   me    you    him   her   it    us    them
```

Форма подлежащего идёт перед глаголом, форма дополнения — после глагола или предлога:

```
I saw her.          She saw me.
Give it to him.     Come with us.
```

После предлога — всегда форма дополнения: `between you and **me**`, но не `between you and I`.

## Притяжательные: две формы, две работы

```
перед существительным   my    your   his   her   its    our   their
самостоятельно          mine  yours  his   hers  -      ours  theirs
```

```
This is my car.        This car is mine.
Her book is here.      This book is hers.
```

Второй столбец нужен, когда существительное и так понятно, — поэтому после `mine` существительного никогда не бывает. `This is mine car` — та ошибка, за которой стоит следить.

Две орфографические ловушки, которые важнее, чем кажутся:

- **`its` против `it's`.** `its` — притяжательное (`the dog and its bone`); `it's` — это `it is`. В притяжательном апострофа нет.
- **`your` против `you're`.** То же деление по той же причине.

## Апостроф у существительных

У людей и животных принадлежность вешается на существительное:

```
Anna's book         the boy's dog
the boys' dogs      (множественное и так на -s, поэтому только апостроф)
the children's toys (нерегулярное множественное, поэтому 's)
```

Для предметов английский предпочитает `of`: `the leg of the table`, а не `the table's leg`.

## Возвратные

```
myself  yourself  himself  herself  itself  ourselves  yourselves  themselves
```

Нужны, когда подлежащее и дополнение — одно лицо: `I hurt myself`, `She taught herself Spanish`. И ещё для усиления: `I did it myself`.

Ловушка в том, что часть английских глаголов не возвратные там, где русские возвратные. `Wash`, `dress`, `shave`, `feel`, `relax`, `concentrate`, `meet` возвратного не берут: `I feel bad`, но не `I feel myself bad` — это значит совсем другое, и лучше так не говорить.

## this, that, these, those

```
близко   this (один)    these (много)
далеко   that (один)    those (много)
```

Близко и далеко — это может быть про место, но также про время и про отношение: `this week` — та неделя, в которой мы сейчас, `that year` — год, который уже кончился.

Они работают и как определители (`this book`), и как самостоятельные местоимения (`This is my book`). И они несут число, поэтому обязаны согласовываться: `these books`, но не `this books`.

summary.en: The tense for what is generally true rather than what is happening now: how the third-person -s works, why do/does appears in questions, and the state verbs that stay in this tense even about right now.
summary.ru: Время для того, что верно вообще, а не происходит сейчас: как работает -s в третьем лице, откуда do/does в вопросах и какие глаголы состояния остаются в этом времени даже про сию минуту.

body.en:
Present Simple is not the tense for "now". It is the tense for things that are true in general — habits, facts, schedules, permanent situations. What is happening at this moment is Present Continuous, and keeping the two apart is the first real decision English grammar asks of you.

## Form

```
I/you/we/they  work
he/she/it      works
```

That `-s` is the only ending, and it is the one most often dropped. Spelling:

```
-s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -o  ->  -es    watch/watches, go/goes, do/does
consonant + -y             ->  -ies   study/studies  (but: play/plays)
have                       ->  has
```

Questions and negatives use `do`/`does`, and once the auxiliary carries the tense the main verb loses the `-s`:

```
Do you work?          I don't work.
Does she work?        She doesn't work.
```

`Does she works?` doubles the marking — the single most common error in this tense. The tense is marked once.

## What it is for

```
Habits and repeated actions:  I get up at seven. She often travels.
Permanent situations:         He lives in Riga. I work for a bank.
General facts:                Water boils at 100C. The sun rises in the east.
Timetables:                   The train leaves at six. The film starts at eight.
```

The timetable use is worth noticing: it talks about the future with a present tense, because a schedule is treated as a standing fact. `The train leaves at six tomorrow` is correct and normal.

It is also the tense of instructions and commentary — recipes, directions, sports commentary, and telling the plot of a film or book: `First you boil the water`, `He passes the ball and scores`.

## Adverbs of frequency

They live before the main verb, but after `be`:

```
I always drink coffee.        I am always late.
She never eats meat.          She is never late.
```

`always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never` sit there. Longer expressions — `every day`, `once a week`, `on Mondays` — go at the end instead: `I go to the gym twice a week`.

## State verbs stay simple

Some verbs describe states rather than actions, and they use Present Simple even when they mean right now. This is why "Present Simple is not about now" needs a caveat:

```
know, understand, remember, forget, believe, think (= have an opinion)
like, love, hate, prefer, want, need
be, have (= own), belong, contain, cost, seem, mean
see, hear, smell, taste
```

So `I know the answer`, not `I am knowing`. `I want coffee`, not `I am wanting`.

A few of these have a second, active meaning, and in that meaning the continuous is fine:

```
I think it's a good idea.     (opinion - state)
I'm thinking about it.        (mental activity - action)
I have a car.                 (own - state)
I'm having lunch.             (eat - action)
This soup tastes good.        (state)
The chef is tasting the soup. (action)
```

`I'm loving it` exists as deliberate informal advertising English; treat it as an exception, not a pattern.
body.ru:
Present Simple — не время для «сейчас». Это время для того, что верно вообще: привычек, фактов, расписаний, постоянных положений дел. То, что происходит в эту минуту, — это Present Continuous, и различить их — первое настоящее решение, которого от вас требует английская грамматика.

## Форма

```
I/you/we/they  work
he/she/it      works
```

Это `-s` — единственное окончание, и именно его чаще всего теряют. Орфография:

```
-s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -o  ->  -es    watch/watches, go/goes, do/does
согласная + -y             ->  -ies   study/studies  (но: play/plays)
have                       ->  has
```

Вопрос и отрицание строятся через `do`/`does`, и как только вспомогательный берёт на себя время, смысловой глагол теряет `-s`:

```
Do you work?          I don't work.
Does she work?        She doesn't work.
```

`Does she works?` помечает время дважды — самая частая ошибка в этом времени. Время помечается один раз.

## Для чего оно

```
Привычки и повторяющиеся действия:  I get up at seven. She often travels.
Постоянные положения дел:            He lives in Riga. I work for a bank.
Общие факты:                         Water boils at 100C. The sun rises in the east.
Расписания:                          The train leaves at six. The film starts at eight.
```

Случай с расписанием стоит заметить: настоящим временем говорят о будущем, потому что расписание считается устойчивым фактом. `The train leaves at six tomorrow` — правильно и обычно.

Это же время инструкций и комментария — рецептов, объяснения дороги, спортивного репортажа и пересказа сюжета: `First you boil the water`, `He passes the ball and scores`.

## Наречия частоты

Живут перед смысловым глаголом, но после `be`:

```
I always drink coffee.        I am always late.
She never eats meat.          She is never late.
```

Там стоят `always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never`. Более длинные выражения — `every day`, `once a week`, `on Mondays` — уходят в конец: `I go to the gym twice a week`.

## Глаголы состояния остаются в простом

Часть глаголов описывает состояния, а не действия, и они стоят в Present Simple даже когда речь про сию минуту. Вот почему к «Present Simple не про сейчас» нужна оговорка:

```
know, understand, remember, forget, believe, think (= иметь мнение)
like, love, hate, prefer, want, need
be, have (= владеть), belong, contain, cost, seem, mean
see, hear, smell, taste
```

Поэтому `I know the answer`, а не `I am knowing`. `I want coffee`, а не `I am wanting`.

У некоторых из них есть второе, деятельное значение — и в нём continuous совершенно нормален:

```
I think it's a good idea.     (мнение - состояние)
I'm thinking about it.        (мыслительная работа - действие)
I have a car.                 (владею - состояние)
I'm having lunch.             (ем - действие)
This soup tastes good.        (состояние)
The chef is tasting the soup. (действие)
```

`I'm loving it` существует как намеренно разговорный рекламный английский; относитесь к нему как к исключению, а не как к образцу.

summary.en: be + -ing for what is in progress, and the choice between the two presents: in progress now or around now, against generally true.
summary.ru: be + -ing для того, что в процессе, и выбор между двумя настоящими: в процессе сейчас или около сейчас против «верно вообще».

body.en:
Present Continuous is `be` plus `-ing`. Since `be` changes and the main verb does not, the whole tense hangs on getting `am/is/are` right — and dropping it is the error to watch, because Russian has no auxiliary to drop.

## Form

```
I am working        I'm working        am I working?
you are working     you're working     are you working?
she is working      she's working      is she working?
```

Negative: `I'm not working`, `she isn't working`.

`-ing` spelling:

```
-e dropped                make/making, write/writing
one vowel + one consonant, stressed  ->  double it    sit/sitting, run/running
-ie -> -y                 lie/lying, die/dying
```

Note `be` needs no `do`: `Are you working?`, never `Do you be working?`

## What it is for

```
Happening right now:        I'm reading a book. Don't call - she's driving.
Around now, not this second: I'm learning Spanish. He's writing a novel.
A temporary situation:      I'm living with my parents until June.
A trend or change:          Prices are rising. The climate is getting warmer.
A planned arrangement:      I'm meeting Anna tomorrow.
```

The second one matters more than it looks. `I'm learning Spanish` does not mean you are learning it at this instant — it means the activity is ongoing over a stretch of time that includes now. `He's writing a novel` is true while he is asleep.

The last one — a fixed arrangement in the future — is covered again in the section on the future, but it is worth seeing here: a present tense used for something scheduled and agreed.

## Always + continuous

With `always`, the continuous stops being neutral and becomes a complaint:

```
He is always losing his keys.       (irritating - too often)
He always loses his keys.           (neutral - a habit)
```

## Choosing between the two presents

The question to ask is what kind of truth you are stating:

```
in progress / temporary  ->  continuous
generally true / permanent -> simple
```

```
I work in a bank.            (my job)
I'm working in a bank.       (for now - temporarily)

She doesn't eat meat.        (vegetarian)
She isn't eating meat.       (right now, or these days)

The bus leaves at six.       (timetable)
The bus is leaving.          (right now, doors closing)
```

And the constraint from the previous section still applies: **state verbs do not take the continuous.** `I know`, `I want`, `I understand`, `I need` — never `I am knowing`. When a state verb appears in `-ing`, it has switched to an action meaning.

```
Do you understand?        not: Are you understanding?
This book belongs to me.  not: is belonging
```
body.ru:
Present Continuous — это `be` плюс `-ing`. Поскольку меняется `be`, а смысловой глагол нет, всё время держится на правильном `am/is/are`, — и его потеря как раз та ошибка, за которой стоит следить: в русском нет вспомогательного глагола, который можно было бы потерять.

## Форма

```
I am working        I'm working        am I working?
you are working     you're working     are you working?
she is working      she's working      is she working?
```

Отрицание: `I'm not working`, `she isn't working`.

Орфография `-ing`:

```
-e отбрасывается                     make/making, write/writing
одна гласная + одна согласная под ударением  ->  удвоение    sit/sitting, run/running
-ie -> -y                            lie/lying, die/dying
```

Заметьте: `be` не нужен `do`: `Are you working?`, но не `Do you be working?`

## Для чего оно

```
Происходит прямо сейчас:            I'm reading a book. Don't call - she's driving.
Около сейчас, не в эту секунду:      I'm learning Spanish. He's writing a novel.
Временное положение дел:             I'm living with my parents until June.
Тенденция, изменение:                Prices are rising. The climate is getting warmer.
Договорённость на будущее:           I'm meeting Anna tomorrow.
```

Второй пункт важнее, чем выглядит. `I'm learning Spanish` не означает, что вы учите его в это мгновение, — означает, что занятие длится на отрезке времени, включающем сейчас. `He's writing a novel` верно и пока он спит.

Последний пункт — назначенная договорённость в будущем — разбирается ещё раз в разделе о будущем, но увидеть его стоит уже здесь: настоящее время для чего-то запланированного и согласованного.

## Always + continuous

С `always` continuous перестаёт быть нейтральным и превращается в жалобу:

```
He is always losing his keys.       (раздражает - слишком часто)
He always loses his keys.           (нейтрально - привычка)
```

## Выбор между двумя настоящими

Спрашивать надо, какого рода истину вы сообщаете:

```
в процессе / временно      ->  continuous
верно вообще / постоянно    ->  simple
```

```
I work in a bank.            (моя работа)
I'm working in a bank.       (пока что - временно)

She doesn't eat meat.        (вегетарианка)
She isn't eating meat.       (сейчас или в эти дни)

The bus leaves at six.       (расписание)
The bus is leaving.          (сейчас, двери закрываются)
```

И ограничение из предыдущего раздела остаётся в силе: **глаголы состояния continuous не берут.** `I know`, `I want`, `I understand`, `I need` — но никогда `I am knowing`. Если глагол состояния появился в `-ing`, значит он переключился в деятельное значение.

```
Do you understand?        не: Are you understanding?
This book belongs to me.  не: is belonging
```

summary.en: The tense for a finished action at a finished time: regular -ed and the irregular list, did in questions, and why a past time marker forces this tense.
summary.ru: Время для законченного действия в законченное время: регулярное -ed и список нерегулярных, did в вопросах и почему указание на прошлое требует именно этого времени.

body.en:
Past Simple describes something finished, at a time that is also finished. It is the default tense for telling a story, and it is where English keeps its irregular verb list.

## Form

Regular verbs add `-ed`, and the form does not change by person:

```
I/you/he/she/we/they  worked
```

Spelling:

```
-e already there  ->  -d       like/liked
consonant + -y    ->  -ied     study/studied  (but: play/played)
one vowel + one consonant, stressed  ->  double it   stop/stopped, plan/planned
```

Irregular verbs have to be learned. The high-frequency ones:

```
be/was,were   go/went     have/had     do/did      say/said
make/made     take/took   get/got      come/came   see/saw
know/knew     think/thought  give/gave  find/found  tell/told
buy/bought    bring/brought  read/read  put/put     cut/cut
```

`read/read` is spelled the same and pronounced differently. `put` and `cut` do not change at all.

## Questions and negatives

`did` carries the tense, so the main verb returns to its plain form — the same rule as `do`/`does` in the present:

```
Did you work?         I didn't work.
Did she go?           She didn't go.
```

`Did you worked?` and `She didn't went` are the errors this rule prevents. Once `did` is there, the past is already marked.

`be` is the exception, as always — it needs no auxiliary:

```
Was he at home?       He wasn't at home.
Were they late?       They weren't late.
```

## When to use it

The signal is a finished past time, stated or understood:

```
yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago, when I was a child
```

```
I saw her yesterday.
He lived in Berlin for five years.   (and no longer does)
Did you call your mother?            (about an occasion now past)
```

A past time marker makes this tense obligatory. `I have seen her yesterday` is wrong for exactly this reason — `yesterday` is a finished time, so Past Simple is the only option. That contrast is the whole subject of the Present Perfect section in the intermediate course; here it is enough to know which side of it you are on.

It is also the tense for a sequence of finished events, which is why narration lives in it:

```
I woke up, made coffee and went out.
```

## used to and would

For habits that are over, `used to` says so explicitly:

```
I used to smoke.            (I don't now)
She used to live here.
```

Questions and negatives run through `did`, and the `d` disappears: `Did you use to smoke?`, `I didn't use to like it`.

`used to` works with both states and repeated actions. `would` also expresses a past habit, but only with actions, not states: `Every summer we would go to the lake` is fine; `I would live in Riga` does not mean you used to live there.
body.ru:
Past Simple описывает нечто законченное в законченное же время. Это время по умолчанию для рассказа, и именно в нём английский держит свой список нерегулярных глаголов.

## Форма

Регулярные глаголы добавляют `-ed`, и форма не меняется по лицам:

```
I/you/he/she/we/they  worked
```

Орфография:

```
-e уже есть        ->  -d       like/liked
согласная + -y     ->  -ied     study/studied  (но: play/played)
одна гласная + одна согласная под ударением  ->  удвоение   stop/stopped, plan/planned
```

Нерегулярные приходится выучить. Самые частотные:

```
be/was,were   go/went     have/had     do/did      say/said
make/made     take/took   get/got      come/came   see/saw
know/knew     think/thought  give/gave  find/found  tell/told
buy/bought    bring/brought  read/read  put/put     cut/cut
```

`read/read` пишется одинаково, а читается по-разному. `put` и `cut` не меняются вовсе.

## Вопрос и отрицание

Время берёт на себя `did`, поэтому смысловой глагол возвращается в исходную форму — то же правило, что с `do`/`does` в настоящем:

```
Did you work?         I didn't work.
Did she go?           She didn't go.
```

`Did you worked?` и `She didn't went` — как раз те ошибки, от которых спасает это правило. Раз есть `did`, прошедшее уже помечено.

`be`, как всегда, исключение — вспомогательный ему не нужен:

```
Was he at home?       He wasn't at home.
Were they late?       They weren't late.
```

## Когда его брать

Признак — законченное прошедшее время, названное или подразумеваемое:

```
yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago, when I was a child
```

```
I saw her yesterday.
He lived in Berlin for five years.   (и больше не живёт)
Did you call your mother?            (о случае, который уже в прошлом)
```

Указание на прошедшее время делает это время обязательным. `I have seen her yesterday` неверно ровно по этой причине: `yesterday` — законченное время, значит Past Simple единственный вариант. Это противопоставление — весь сюжет раздела про Present Perfect в курсе intermediate; здесь достаточно понимать, на какой вы стороне.

Это же время для цепочки законченных событий — поэтому в нём и живёт повествование:

```
I woke up, made coffee and went out.
```

## used to и would

Для привычек, которые кончились, `used to` говорит об этом прямо:

```
I used to smoke.            (сейчас нет)
She used to live here.
```

Вопрос и отрицание идут через `did`, и `d` при этом исчезает: `Did you use to smoke?`, `I didn't use to like it`.

`used to` работает и с состояниями, и с повторяющимися действиями. `would` тоже выражает прошлую привычку, но только с действиями, не с состояниями: `Every summer we would go to the lake` — нормально; а `I would live in Riga` не означает, что вы там жили.

summary.ru: was/were + -ing для того, что длилось в прошлом, и связка с Past Simple, которую явно выражают when и while.

body.en:
Past Continuous is `was`/`were` plus `-ing`. On its own it is rarely interesting; its job is almost always to be the background against which a Past Simple event happens.

## Form

```
I/he/she/it   was working
you/we/they   were working
```

```
Was she working?      She wasn't working.
Were they working?    They weren't working.
```

Two forms of `was/were` to get right, and no `did` anywhere — `be` inverts on its own.

## The background and the event

This is the pattern the tense exists for. The longer action goes in the continuous, the shorter one that interrupts it goes in the simple:

```
I was reading when the phone rang.
She was cooking when I arrived.
```

Both halves are past; the difference is that one was in progress and the other happened at a point inside it. Reverse the tenses and you reverse the meaning:

```
When I arrived, she was cooking.     (she started before I got there)
When I arrived, she cooked.          (she started after - my arrival came first)
```

## when and while

They mark the two halves, and they usually take different tenses:

```
while  +  continuous     (the longer action)
when   +  simple         (the shorter event)
```

```
While I was walking home, I met Anna.
I was walking home when I met Anna.
```

Both sentences say the same thing. Note the comma: when the `while`/`when` clause comes first, a comma separates the halves; when it comes second, there is none.

Two actions that were both in progress at the same time both go in the continuous, usually with `while`:

```
I was cooking while she was watching TV.
```

## Other uses

```
Setting a scene:        It was raining. People were hurrying home.
A temporary past state: I was living in Riga at the time.
Two things at once:     He was talking on the phone and driving.
Always + complaint:     She was always arriving late.
```

The scene-setting use is why stories often open in the continuous and then switch to the simple once things start happening.

## What it is not for

It does not describe a finished, complete action. `I was reading the book` says nothing about whether you finished it; `I read the book` says you did. So a completed sequence stays in the simple:

```
I got up, had breakfast and left.
not: I was getting up, was having breakfast...
```

And **state verbs still refuse the continuous**, in the past exactly as in the present:

```
I knew the answer.        not: I was knowing
She wanted to leave.      not: was wanting
```

Past Continuous — это `was`/`were` плюс `-ing`. Сам по себе он редко интересен; его работа почти всегда — быть фоном, на котором происходит событие в Past Simple.

## Форма

```
I/he/she/it   was working
you/we/they   were working
```

```
Was she working?      She wasn't working.
Were they working?    They weren't working.
```

Нужно не путать две формы `was/were`, и никакого `did` здесь нет — `be` переставляется сам.

## Фон и событие

Это та схема, ради которой время и существует. Более длинное действие идёт в continuous, короткое, которое его прерывает, — в simple:

```
I was reading when the phone rang.
She was cooking when I arrived.
```

Обе половины в прошлом; разница в том, что одно длилось, а другое случилось в точке внутри него. Поменяйте времена местами — поменяется смысл:

```
When I arrived, she was cooking.     (начала до моего прихода)
When I arrived, she cooked.          (начала после - сначала пришёл я)
```

## when и while

Они помечают две половины и обычно берут разные времена:

```
while  +  continuous     (длинное действие)
when   +  simple         (короткое событие)
```

```
While I was walking home, I met Anna.
I was walking home when I met Anna.
```

Оба предложения говорят одно и то же. Обратите внимание на запятую: если часть с `while`/`when` стоит первой, запятая половины разделяет; если второй — запятой нет.

Два действия, которые оба длились одновременно, оба идут в continuous, обычно с `while`:

```
I was cooking while she was watching TV.
```

## Другие употребления

```
Задать обстановку:          It was raining. People were hurrying home.
Временное прошлое состояние: I was living in Riga at the time.
Два дела одновременно:       He was talking on the phone and driving.
Always + жалоба:             She was always arriving late.
```

Из-за первого пункта рассказы часто и открываются continuous, а потом переходят в simple, когда начинают происходить события.

## Для чего оно не годится

Оно не описывает законченное, завершённое действие. `I was reading the book` ничего не говорит о том, дочитали ли вы; `I read the book` говорит, что дочитали. Поэтому завершённая цепочка остаётся в simple:

```
I got up, had breakfast and left.
не: I was getting up, was having breakfast...
```

И **глаголы состояния по-прежнему continuous не берут** — в прошедшем ровно так же, как в настоящем:

```
I knew the answer.        не: I was knowing
She wanted to leave.      не: was wanting
```

summary.en: English has no future tense, it has four ways of talking about the future: will, going to, present continuous and present simple, each carrying a different reason for saying it.
summary.ru: Будущего времени в английском нет — есть четыре способа говорить о будущем: will, going to, present continuous и present simple, и каждый несёт своё основание.

body.en:
English has no future tense in the way it has a past tense: there is no ending you add. Instead there are four constructions, and choosing between them is not about *when* the thing happens but about *why you are saying it* — is it a decision, a plan, a prediction, a timetable?

## will

`will` plus the plain verb, same for every person, contracted to `'ll`:

```
I will go / I'll go        will you go?        I won't go
```

Use it for:

```
A decision made as you speak:  OK, I'll help you.
A prediction or opinion:       I think it will rain. She'll like it.
An offer or promise:           I'll carry that. I'll call you tomorrow.
A refusal:                     I won't do it.
```

The first one is the key contrast with `going to`. `will` is the tense of choosing on the spot: the phone rings and you say `I'll get it`.

## going to

`be going to` plus the plain verb:

```
I'm going to study medicine.       Are you going to tell her?
```

Use it for:

```
A plan or intention already made:  I'm going to study medicine.
A prediction based on evidence:     Look at those clouds - it's going to rain.
```

Both halves of the contrast with `will` sit here:

```
The phone's ringing.  -  I'll answer it.        (deciding now)
I'm going to call her tonight.                  (decided earlier)

I think it'll rain.                             (my opinion)
It's going to rain.                             (I can see the clouds)
```

## Present Continuous

For a fixed arrangement — something agreed, with a time and usually another person involved:

```
I'm meeting Anna at six.
We're flying to London on Monday.
```

The line between this and `going to` is thin, and often either works. The difference is that the continuous implies the arrangement is settled — booked, agreed, in the diary — while `going to` only needs the intention to exist.

## Present Simple

For timetables and schedules — things fixed by an institution rather than by you:

```
The train leaves at six.
The film starts at eight.
Term begins in September.
```

This is why `The train leaves tomorrow` is right and `The train will leave tomorrow` sounds like a prediction about a train with a mind of its own.

## After when, if, before, until

The one rule that catches everyone: **no `will` in a time or conditional clause.** English uses a present tense there, even though the meaning is future:

```
I'll call you when I arrive.        not: when I will arrive
If it rains, we'll stay in.         not: if it will rain
Wait until she comes back.
```

The future is marked once, in the main clause. This applies after `when, if, as soon as, before, after, until, unless`.

## Choosing, in short

```
deciding right now           ->  will
already intended             ->  going to
arranged, in the diary       ->  present continuous
on a timetable               ->  present simple
opinion about the future     ->  will
evidence in front of you     ->  going to
```

Будущего времени в английском нет в том смысле, в каком есть прошедшее: никакого окончания вы не добавляете. Вместо этого есть четыре конструкции, и выбор между ними — не про то, *когда* случится событие, а про то, *на каком основании вы это говорите*: это решение, план, предсказание или расписание?

## will

`will` плюс глагол в исходной форме, одинаково для всех лиц, сокращается до `'ll`:

```

```

```
Решения, принятого в момент речи:  OK, I'll help you.
Предсказания или мнения:            I think it will rain. She'll like it.
Предложения помощи или обещания:    I'll carry that. I'll call you tomorrow.
Отказа:                             I won't do it.
```

Первый пункт — ключевое противопоставление с `going to`. `will` — время решения на месте: звонит телефон, и вы говорите `I'll get it`.

```

```

```
Плана или намерения, уже принятого:  I'm going to study medicine.
Предсказания по видимым признакам:    Look at those clouds - it's going to rain.
```

Обе половины противопоставления с `will` лежат здесь:

```

I'm going to call her tonight.                  (решил раньше)

I think it'll rain.                             (моё мнение)
It's going to rain.                             (я вижу тучи)
```

## Present Continuous

Для назначенной договорённости — того, что согласовано, со временем и обычно с участием другого человека:

```
I'm meeting Anna at six.
We're flying to London on Monday.
```

Граница с `going to` тонкая, и часто годится и то и то. Разница в том, что continuous подразумевает: договорённость улажена — забронировано, согласовано, записано в календарь, — тогда как `going to` требует только наличия намерения.

## Present Simple

Для расписаний — того, что закреплено учреждением, а не вами:

```
The train leaves at six.
The film starts at eight.
Term begins in September.
```

Поэтому `The train leaves tomorrow` — правильно, а `The train will leave tomorrow` звучит как предсказание о поезде, у которого есть своя воля.

## После when, if, before, until

Единственное правило, на котором спотыкаются все: **никакого `will` в придаточном времени или условия.** Английский ставит там настоящее время, хотя смысл будущий:

```
I'll call you when I arrive.        не: when I will arrive
If it rains, we'll stay in.         не: if it will rain
Wait until she comes back.
```

Будущее помечается один раз — в главной части. Это касается `when, if, as soon as, before, after, until, unless`.

## Выбор коротко

```
решаю прямо сейчас            ->  will
уже намеревался               ->  going to
договорено, записано          ->  present continuous
по расписанию                 ->  present simple
мнение о будущем              ->  will
признаки прямо перед глазами  ->  going to
```

summary.en: Modal verbs break the ordinary rules: no -s, no do, no to. What can, must, should and have to each mean, and why must not and don't have to are opposites.
summary.ru: Модальные глаголы нарушают обычные правила: без -s, без do, без to. Что означают can, must, should и have to и почему must not и don't have to — противоположности.

body.en:
Modal verbs say how the speaker relates to the action — possible, necessary, advisable — rather than describing an action themselves. Grammatically they are a closed club with their own rules.

## The rules they all share

```
no -s in the third person:   she can, not she cans
no do in questions:          Can you? not Do you can?
no to after them:            I can swim, not I can to swim
never two in a row:          not: I will can
```

That last one is why the future of `can` has to be borrowed: `I'll **be able to** swim`.

## can

```
Ability:      I can swim. She can speak three languages.
Permission:   Can I go? You can use my phone.
Possibility:  It can get cold here in winter.
Requests:     Can you help me?
```

The past of ability is `could`: `I could swim when I was five`. `could` is also a softer, more polite `can` for requests: `Could you help me?`

For ability in other tenses, `be able to` fills in: `I haven't been able to sleep`, `I'll be able to come`.

## must and have to

Both express necessity, and in the present they are often interchangeable. The difference is where the pressure comes from:

```
I must finish this.        (I impose it on myself)
I have to finish this.     (circumstances or someone else impose it)
```

`must` has no past and no future of its own, so `have to` covers those:

```
I had to leave early.        not: I musted
I'll have to leave early.
```

`have to` is an ordinary verb, so it takes `do` in questions and negatives — unlike `must`:

```
Do you have to go?          Must you go?
I don't have to go.         I mustn't go.
```

## The negatives are opposites

This is the single most important thing in the section:

```
You mustn't go.        =  it is forbidden - do not go
You don't have to go.  =  it is not necessary - go if you like
```

They are not two ways of saying the same thing. Mixing them up reverses the instruction.

## should

Advice and opinion, weaker than `must`:

```
You should see a doctor.          You shouldn't work so hard.
Should I call her?
```

`ought to` means the same and is slightly more formal — and it is the one modal that keeps its `to`.

`had better` is stronger than `should` and carries a warning: `You'd better leave now` implies something bad follows if you do not.

## In short

```
can        ability, permission, possibility
could      past ability, polite request
must       necessity from the speaker, strong deduction
have to    necessity from outside
mustn't    forbidden
don't have to  not necessary
should     advice
```
body.ru:
Модальные глаголы сообщают, как говорящий относится к действию — возможно, необходимо, желательно, — а не описывают действие сами. Грамматически это закрытый клуб со своими правилами.

## Правила, общие для всех

```
никакого -s в третьем лице:   she can, а не she cans
никакого do в вопросе:         Can you? а не Do you can?
никакого to после них:         I can swim, а не I can to swim
никогда два подряд:            нельзя: I will can
```

Из последнего следует, что будущее у `can` приходится занимать: `I'll **be able to** swim`.

## can

```
Умение:          I can swim. She can speak three languages.
Разрешение:      Can I go? You can use my phone.
Возможность:     It can get cold here in winter.
Просьба:         Can you help me?
```

Прошедшее от умения — `could`: `I could swim when I was five`. `could` — ещё и более мягкий, вежливый `can` для просьб: `Could you help me?`

Для умения в остальных временах подставляется `be able to`: `I haven't been able to sleep`, `I'll be able to come`.

## must и have to

Оба выражают необходимость, и в настоящем времени часто взаимозаменяемы. Разница в том, откуда идёт давление:

```
I must finish this.        (я налагаю это на себя сам)
I have to finish this.     (налагают обстоятельства или кто-то другой)
```

У `must` нет своего прошедшего и будущего, поэтому их закрывает `have to`:

```
I had to leave early.        не: I musted
I'll have to leave early.
```

`have to` — обычный глагол, поэтому в вопросе и отрицании он берёт `do`, в отличие от `must`:

```
Do you have to go?          Must you go?
I don't have to go.         I mustn't go.
```

## Отрицания у них противоположны

Это самое важное в разделе:

```
You mustn't go.        =  запрещено - не ходи
You don't have to go.  =  не обязательно - иди, если хочешь
```

Это не два способа сказать одно и то же. Спутать их — значит вывернуть указание наизнанку.

## should

Совет и мнение, слабее чем `must`:

```
You should see a doctor.          You shouldn't work so hard.
Should I call her?
```

`ought to` значит то же и чуть формальнее — и это единственный модальный, который сохраняет своё `to`.

`had better` сильнее `should` и несёт предупреждение: `You'd better leave now` подразумевает, что иначе случится что-то плохое.

## Коротко

```
can        умение, разрешение, возможность
could      прошлое умение, вежливая просьба
must       необходимость от говорящего, сильное предположение
have to    необходимость извне
mustn't    запрещено
don't have to  не обязательно
should     совет
```

summary.en: Adjectives never take a plural, adverbs are mostly adjective plus -ly, and comparison splits by syllable count into -er/-est and more/most.
summary.ru: Прилагательные не имеют множественного числа, наречия — это в основном прилагательное плюс -ly, а сравнение делится по числу слогов на -er/-est и more/most.

body.en:
Adjectives describe nouns, adverbs describe verbs, and English keeps them apart more strictly than Russian does. Both then feed into one system of comparison.

## Adjectives do not agree

An English adjective has exactly one form. It never takes a plural and never changes for gender:

```
a red car        two red cars       not: two reds cars
```

It goes before the noun, or after `be`, `seem`, `look`, `feel`, `become`:

```
an interesting book        The book is interesting.
She looks tired.           It seems easy.
```

Where several adjectives stack up, the order is fixed and native speakers follow it without thinking: **opinion - size - age - shape - colour - origin - material - purpose**.

```
a nice big old round brown Italian wooden dining table
```

Nobody uses all eight at once, but `a big red car` is right and `a red big car` sounds wrong.

## Adverbs

Most are the adjective plus `-ly`:

```
quick/quickly    slow/slowly    careful/carefully
easy/easily      (consonant + -y -> -ily)
```

Some are the same word in both jobs — `fast`, `hard`, `late`, `early`:

```
a fast car / he drives fast        not: fastly
```

And two pairs are worth learning outright:

```
good  ->  well       She is a good singer. She sings well.
hard  ->  hardly     I work hard. I hardly work.   (= almost not at all)
late  ->  lately     He arrived late. I haven't seen him lately. (= recently)
```

`hardly` is not the adverb of `hard`; it is a near-negative, and confusing the two says the opposite of what you meant.

## Comparison

The split is by length:

```
one syllable            -er / -est      big/bigger/the biggest
two syllables in -y     -ier / -iest    happy/happier/the happiest
two or more syllables   more / most     expensive/more expensive/the most expensive
```

Spelling follows the same habits as elsewhere: `big/bigger` doubles the consonant, `nice/nicer` drops the `e`.

The irregulars are few and frequent:

```
good/better/the best        bad/worse/the worst
far/further/the furthest    little/less/the least
many, much/more/the most
```

## than, as, the

Comparatives take `than`; superlatives take `the`:

```
She is taller than me.
This is the most expensive one.
```

Never both markers at once: `more cheaper` and `more better` are the errors to avoid — the comparative is marked once.

For equality, `as ... as`, and its negative:

```
He is as tall as his father.
She isn't as old as she looks.
```

`too` and `enough` sit on either side of "the right amount", and they land on different sides of the word:

```
too + adjective            This coffee is too hot.
adjective + enough         It isn't hot enough.
enough + noun              I don't have enough money.
```
body.ru:
Прилагательные описывают существительные, наречия — глаголы, и английский разделяет их строже, чем русский. Дальше оба вливаются в одну систему сравнения.

## Прилагательные не согласуются

У английского прилагательного ровно одна форма. Оно не имеет множественного числа и не меняется по родам:

```
a red car        two red cars       не: two reds cars
```

Стоит перед существительным либо после `be`, `seem`, `look`, `feel`, `become`:

```
an interesting book        The book is interesting.
She looks tired.           It seems easy.
```

Когда прилагательных скапливается несколько, порядок закреплён, и носители следуют ему не задумываясь: **оценка - размер - возраст - форма - цвет - происхождение - материал - назначение**.

```
a nice big old round brown Italian wooden dining table
```

Все восемь сразу никто не употребляет, но `a big red car` — правильно, а `a red big car` звучит неверно.

## Наречия

Большинство — это прилагательное плюс `-ly`:

```
quick/quickly    slow/slowly    careful/carefully
easy/easily      (согласная + -y -> -ily)
```

Некоторые совпадают в обеих ролях — `fast`, `hard`, `late`, `early`:

```
a fast car / he drives fast        не: fastly
```

А две пары стоит просто выучить:

```
good  ->  well       She is a good singer. She sings well.
hard  ->  hardly     I work hard. I hardly work.   (= почти совсем не работаю)
late  ->  lately     He arrived late. I haven't seen him lately. (= в последнее время)
```

`hardly` — не наречие от `hard`, а почти-отрицание, и спутать их значит сказать противоположное задуманному.

## Сравнение

Деление — по длине:

```
один слог                 -er / -est      big/bigger/the biggest
два слога на -y           -ier / -iest    happy/happier/the happiest
два слога и больше        more / most     expensive/more expensive/the most expensive
```

Орфография следует тем же привычкам, что и везде: `big/bigger` удваивает согласную, `nice/nicer` теряет `e`.

Нерегулярных мало, и все частотные:

```
good/better/the best        bad/worse/the worst
far/further/the furthest    little/less/the least
many, much/more/the most
```

## than, as, the

Сравнительная степень берёт `than`, превосходная — `the`:

```
She is taller than me.
This is the most expensive one.
```

Никогда оба показателя одновременно: `more cheaper` и `more better` — как раз те ошибки, которых надо избегать. Степень помечается один раз.

Для равенства — `as ... as` и его отрицание:

```
He is as tall as his father.
She isn't as old as she looks.
```

`too` и `enough` стоят по обе стороны от «сколько нужно», и встают они с разных сторон слова:

```
too + прилагательное            This coffee is too hot.
прилагательное + enough         It isn't hot enough.
enough + существительное        I don't have enough money.
```

summary.ru: in, on и at для времени и для места, разложенные по размеру и точности, плюс устойчивые выражения, которые выгоднее выучить, чем выводить.

body.en:
Prepositions are where word-for-word translation fails most reliably, because the two languages divide up space and time differently. The three central ones follow a pattern worth seeing, and the rest are vocabulary.

## Time

The pattern is precision: `at` for a point, `on` for a day, `in` for anything longer.

```
at   a clock time, a mealtime, night      at 6 o'clock, at lunch, at night
on   a day or a date                      on Monday, on 5 May, on my birthday
in   a month, season, year, century       in July, in winter, in 2019
     part of a day                        in the morning, in the evening
```

`at night` breaks the pattern — everything else about a part of the day takes `in`. Learn it as an exception.

No preposition at all before `next`, `last`, `this`, `every`:

```
I'll see you next week.        not: on next week
I saw her last Monday.
```

`in` also means "after this much time": `I'll be back in ten minutes`.

`for` and `since` measure duration and starting point:

```
for a period    for two hours, for three years
since a point   since Monday, since 2019, since I was a child
```

## Place

The same three, arranged by how enclosed the thing is:

```
at   a point or a place treated as a point   at the door, at the bus stop, at school
on   a surface or a line                     on the table, on the wall, on the second floor
in   inside something with boundaries        in the box, in Riga, in the car
```

The contrast worth drilling is what the same noun does with different prepositions:

```
in the corner (of a room)     at the corner (of a street)
in bed (sleeping)             on the bed (sitting on top)
in the picture                on the picture (physically on the paper)
```

Vehicles split oddly: `in a car` and `in a taxi`, but `on a bus`, `on a train`, `on a plane`, `on a bike`. The rough logic is whether you can walk about inside.

## Movement

`to` marks the destination:

```
I'm going to the shop.        She moved to Berlin.
```

But `home` takes nothing: `I'm going home`, never `to home`. And `arrive` takes `at` or `in`, never `to`:

```
arrive at the station         arrive in Riga
```

## Fixed expressions

These do not follow from the rules and are better memorised whole:

```
at   at home, at work, at school, at the weekend, at first, at last
on   on foot, on holiday, on time, on the phone, on TV, on the left
in   in time, in the end, in fact, in a hurry, in the middle
by   by car, by bus, by train, by mistake, by accident
```

Two pairs that look interchangeable and are not:

```
on time  =  punctually, at the arranged time
in time   =  early enough, with room to spare

at the end  =  at the point where something finishes
in the end   =  finally, after everything
```

Предлоги — то место, где пословный перевод подводит надёжнее всего: два языка делят пространство и время по-разному. Три главных предлога следуют схеме, которую стоит увидеть, остальное — лексика.

## Время

Схема — про точность: `at` для точки, `on` для дня, `in` для всего, что длиннее.

```
at   время по часам, приём пищи, night     at 6 o'clock, at lunch, at night
on   день или дата                         on Monday, on 5 May, on my birthday
in   месяц, сезон, год, век                in July, in winter, in 2019
     часть суток                           in the morning, in the evening
```

`at night` схему ломает — всё остальное про части суток берёт `in`. Это надо запомнить как исключение.

Совсем без предлога — перед `next`, `last`, `this`, `every`:

```
I'll see you next week.        не: on next week
I saw her last Monday.
```

`in` означает ещё и «через столько-то времени»: `I'll be back in ten minutes`.

`for` и `since` меряют длительность и точку начала:

```
for — период        for two hours, for three years
since — точка       since Monday, since 2019, since I was a child
```

## Место

Те же три, разложенные по степени замкнутости:

```
at   точка или место, взятое как точка      at the door, at the bus stop, at school
on   поверхность или линия                  on the table, on the wall, on the second floor
in   внутри чего-то с границами             in the box, in Riga, in the car
```

Отрабатывать стоит противопоставление: что делает одно и то же существительное с разными предлогами.

```
in the corner (комнаты)       at the corner (улицы)
in bed (спит)                 on the bed (сидит сверху)
in the picture                on the picture (физически на бумаге)
```

Транспорт делится странно: `in a car` и `in a taxi`, но `on a bus`, `on a train`, `on a plane`, `on a bike`. Приблизительная логика — можно ли внутри ходить.

## Движение

`to` помечает пункт назначения:

```
I'm going to the shop.        She moved to Berlin.
```

Но `home` не берёт ничего: `I'm going home`, но не `to home`. А `arrive` берёт `at` или `in`, но никогда `to`:

```
arrive at the station         arrive in Riga
```

## Устойчивые выражения

Из правил они не выводятся, и их лучше запомнить целиком:

```
at   at home, at work, at school, at the weekend, at first, at last
on   on foot, on holiday, on time, on the phone, on TV, on the left
in   in time, in the end, in fact, in a hurry, in the middle
by   by car, by bus, by train, by mistake, by accident
```

Две пары, которые выглядят взаимозаменяемыми, но не являются:

```
on time  =  точно в назначенное время
in time   =  достаточно рано, с запасом

at the end  =  в точке, где что-то заканчивается
in the end   =  в конце концов, после всего
```

summary.en: Which quantifier a noun can take depends on whether it is countable, and the some/any split depends on whether the sentence is positive, negative or a question.
summary.ru: Какой квантификатор берёт существительное, зависит от исчисляемости, а выбор между some и any — от того, утверждение это, отрицание или вопрос.

body.en:
Quantifiers say how much or how many. Which one you may use is decided by the countable/uncountable split, so this section only makes sense on top of that one.

## some and any

The rough rule is by sentence type:

```
some   positive statements     I have some money. There are some chairs.
any    negatives and questions Do you have any money? I don't have any.
```

Both work with plurals and with uncountables, and neither takes a singular countable noun.

Two exceptions matter, because they are common:

**`some` in questions when you expect yes** — offers and requests:

```
Would you like some coffee?        (offering - I expect you to say yes)
Could you give me some water?
```

**`any` in a positive sentence meaning "it doesn't matter which"**:

```
Take any seat you like.
Any student can answer that.
```

`no` and `none` are the negative forms. `no` goes before a noun, `none` stands alone:

```
I have no money.          How much is left? - None.
```

Note that `I don't have any money` and `I have no money` mean the same; using both at once would be the double negative English forbids.

## much and many

```
many  +  countable plural     many books, how many books?
much  +  uncountable          much time, how much time?
```

In positive statements both sound formal, and `a lot of` is what people actually say:

```
I have a lot of work.        (natural)
I have much work.            (stiff - avoid)
```

`a lot of` and `lots of` work with both types, which is why they are the safe default. The verb still agrees with the noun, not with `lot`:

```
A lot of people are waiting.       (people - plural)
A lot of time was wasted.          (time - uncountable)
```

## a few and a little

Same split, and this is the pair most often mixed up:

```
a few     +  countable     a few friends, a few days
a little  +  uncountable   a little money, a little time
```

Dropping the `a` changes the attitude, not the amount:

```
I have a few friends.      (some - positive)
I have few friends.        (not many - negative, almost a complaint)

I have a little time.      (some - positive)
I have little time.        (hardly any - negative)
```

`few` and `little` without the article are formal; in speech people say `not many` and `not much` instead.

## a few more

```
all / most        of a whole group      most people, all the students
both / either / neither   of exactly two   both books, neither answer
every / each      one by one            every day, each student  (+ singular verb!)
```

`every` and `each` take a singular noun and a singular verb, which trips people up because the meaning feels plural: `Every student **has** a book`, not `have`.
body.ru:
Квантификаторы говорят, сколько чего. Какой из них можно взять, решает деление на исчисляемые и неисчисляемые, так что этот раздел имеет смысл только поверх того.

## some и any

Грубое правило — по типу предложения:

```
some   утверждения              I have some money. There are some chairs.
any    отрицания и вопросы      Do you have any money? I don't have any.
```

Оба работают с множественным числом и с неисчисляемыми, и ни один не берёт исчисляемое в единственном.

Два исключения важны, потому что они частотны.

**`some` в вопросе, когда ожидаешь «да»** — предложения и просьбы:

```
Would you like some coffee?        (предлагаю - жду, что вы согласитесь)
Could you give me some water?
```

**`any` в утверждении в значении «любой, неважно какой»**:

```
Take any seat you like.
Any student can answer that.
```

`no` и `none` — отрицательные формы. `no` идёт перед существительным, `none` стоит самостоятельно:

```
I have no money.          How much is left? - None.
```

Заметьте, что `I don't have any money` и `I have no money` значат одно и то же; взять оба сразу означало бы то двойное отрицание, которое английский запрещает.

## much и many

```
many  +  исчисляемое множественное    many books, how many books?
much  +  неисчисляемое                much time, how much time?
```

В утверждениях оба звучат формально, а говорят на самом деле `a lot of`:

```
I have a lot of work.        (естественно)
I have much work.            (тяжеловесно - лучше не так)
```

`a lot of` и `lots of` работают с обоими типами — поэтому они и безопасный выбор по умолчанию. Глагол при этом согласуется с существительным, а не с `lot`:

```
A lot of people are waiting.       (people - множественное)
A lot of time was wasted.          (time - неисчисляемое)
```

## a few и a little

То же деление, и это пара, которую путают чаще всего:

```
a few     +  исчисляемое      a few friends, a few days
a little  +  неисчисляемое    a little money, a little time
```

Потеря `a` меняет не количество, а отношение к нему:

```
I have a few friends.      (несколько - положительно)
I have few friends.        (мало - отрицательно, почти жалоба)

I have a little time.      (немного - положительно)
I have little time.        (почти нет - отрицательно)
```

`few` и `little` без артикля формальны; в речи вместо них говорят `not many` и `not much`.

## Ещё несколько

```
all / most               о целой группе        most people, all the students
both / either / neither  ровно о двух          both books, neither answer
every / each             по одному             every day, each student  (+ глагол в единственном!)
```

`every` и `each` берут существительное и глагол в единственном числе, и на этом спотыкаются, потому что смысл ощущается множественным: `Every student **has** a book`, а не `have`.
